name: Design a Cluster Membership and Failure Detection Service
intent: Let every node in a cluster of thousands know, within seconds, which other nodes are alive, without a central monitor, without a flood of heartbeats, and without declaring healthy-but-slow nodes dead.
codeTitle: SWIM-style probing with suspicion and a hash ring
finalIntro: A node crashes, a second node freezes in a garbage-collection pause, and the cluster tells the two apart.
prompt: Design the membership layer under a distributed database such as Cassandra, Consul or Redis Cluster. A cluster has from 10 to 5,000 nodes that join, leave and crash. Every node must know which other nodes are alive so it can route requests and place data. Failures must be noticed in seconds, a slow node must not be mistaken for a dead one, and the layer must keep working when the network drops packets or splits in two.
functional: Detect when a node crashes or becomes unreachable
Tell every node about the failure, and about every join and graceful leave
Let a new node join through a few well-known seed nodes
Give every node a membership list that decides where each key lives on the hash ring
Let a wrongly suspected node prove that it is alive
Expose the list of members and its changes to the application
nonFunctional: A crash is known to every node within about 20 seconds at 100 nodes and within well under a minute at 5,000
The load per node stays about constant as the cluster grows, rather than growing with the number of nodes
A pause of a few seconds from garbage collection, or 5% packet loss, does not cause a false death
No single node is needed for the cluster to notice failures, so there is no single point of failure
The views of different nodes converge without a coordinator, and temporary disagreement is tolerated
Data does not move for a false alarm, and a partition must not leave two sides both believing they own the same keys

firstAttempt.text: A central monitor holds the list of nodes in a config file and pings each one every second. If a node misses three pings, the monitor marks it dead and pushes a new list to everyone. Every node asks the monitor for the list.
limits: The monitor is a single point of failure, and if it dies nobody notices anything else dying
One machine pinging thousands of nodes every second becomes the bottleneck, and its own network trouble looks like thousands of failures
The monitor sees the nodes, but the nodes may not see each other, so its view can differ from what a node experiences
Three missed pings is a fixed rule, so a short garbage-collection pause is treated like a crash
A new node needs someone to edit the config file, and the list pushed to thousands of nodes arrives at different times

steps.title: Let the nodes watch each other instead of one monitor
steps.problem: A central monitor is one machine that must stay alive and see everything, and no single viewpoint tells a node what its own neighbours experience.
steps.fix: Every node keeps the list of members and sends a small heartbeat to every other node each second. A node that has heard nothing from a peer for a timeout, say three seconds, declares that peer dead on its own. No node is special, so no node is a single point of failure, and the verdict reflects what this node itself can reach.
steps.tradeoff: Detection is fast, simple and decentralised. The cost is quadratic, because N nodes each sending to N-1 peers is N(N-1) messages per second: a thousand nodes make a million heartbeats per second, and every node does a thousand sends and receives per second. It is fine for a dozen nodes and impossible for thousands, and every pair of nodes is a separate chance for a false alarm.

steps.title: Probe one random peer per round, and ask others to help
steps.problem: All-to-all heartbeats cost O(N) per node (in proportion to the cluster size), so the monitoring itself becomes the load as the cluster grows.
steps.fix: Use SWIM (a protocol for scalable failure detection). In every protocol period of about one second, each node picks one other node, usually from a shuffled list so that every node is picked within N periods, and sends it a ping over UDP. If no ack arrives in time, the node does not give up. It asks k other nodes, say three, to ping the target for it and report back. Those paths use different network routes, so a lossy link between the two original nodes does not count as a death. Only if every indirect probe also fails does the node doubt the target.
steps.tradeoff: The cost per node is constant, about two messages per second whatever the size of the cluster, and a failed node is probed by someone within about 1.6 periods on average. Each probe is only one node's opinion about one peer, so a single wrong opinion must not become a verdict without a further step.

steps.title: Add a suspicion state, incarnation numbers and adaptive timeouts
steps.problem: A node frozen for four seconds by a garbage-collection pause, or behind a congested link, looks identical to a crashed node, and declaring it dead moves its data for nothing.
steps.fix: A failed probe only moves the target to suspect, not to dead, and that news is spread. The suspect has a suspicion timeout, a few seconds scaled with log N, to prove it is alive. A live node that hears it is suspected raises its incarnation number, a counter only it can increase, and announces alive with the higher number, which overrides the suspicion everywhere. Only a suspect that stays silent for the whole timeout is declared dead. For heartbeat-based detectors, a phi-accrual detector replaces a fixed timeout with a suspicion level computed from the history of arrival times, so it adapts to a slow or jittery network, and nodes that find themselves slow back off before accusing others.
steps.tradeoff: False alarms drop sharply, because the accused gets a chance to answer. The price is detection time: the suspicion timeout is added to the time to the first doubt, so a real crash takes several seconds longer to confirm. Every setting trades speed against accuracy, and a pause longer than the timeout is still taken for a death.

steps.title: Spread membership changes on the messages already being sent
steps.problem: Detecting a failure is not enough: every one of thousands of nodes has to learn about it, and a broadcast from one node would make that node a bottleneck and could be lost.
steps.fix: Each node keeps a small buffer of recent membership updates: suspect, alive with an incarnation number, dead, joined and left. Every ping, ack and indirect probe carries a few of them, and each update is sent about 4 times log10 N times before it expires. The news spreads like an epidemic: each node that learns it passes it on, so the number of informed nodes roughly doubles every round and everyone knows after about log2 N rounds plus a short tail. A conflict between two updates about the same node is settled by the incarnation number, then by the rule that dead beats suspect beats alive at the same number.
steps.tradeoff: There are no extra messages, the load is balanced, and convergence takes O(log N) rounds, so about 6 rounds at 64 nodes and about 15 at 5,000, on top of the suspicion timeout. Views are only eventually consistent, so two nodes can briefly disagree, and an update that is lost on every attempt leaves a node out of date, so a periodic full-state exchange is also needed.

steps.title: Join through seed nodes and sync full state now and then
steps.problem: A brand-new node knows nobody, a node that restarts has a stale list, and dissemination by piggybacking can leave a straggler behind.
steps.fix: A small set of seed nodes, found through configuration or a DNS name, are the entry points. A joining node contacts one, receives the full member list in one exchange (a push-pull sync over TCP), and announces itself with a joined update. A graceful leave sends a left update before the process exits, so the cluster skips the suspicion wait. Every so often, say every 30 seconds, each node does a full push-pull sync with one random peer, which repairs any difference that piggybacking missed.
steps.tradeoff: Joins are automatic, and stale views heal on their own. The seeds are only a way in and are not needed for failure detection, but a node that can reach none of them cannot join. The full sync costs O(N) bytes per exchange, so its period is a deliberate trade against the freshness of the straggler repair.

steps.title: Drive the hash ring from the list, and be careful about partitions
steps.problem: The membership list is only useful if it places keys. A false alarm that moves data wastes bandwidth, and a network partition can leave two groups that each think the other is dead.
steps.fix: Every node builds the same consistent-hash ring from its member list, with many virtual nodes each, so removing one node moves only the keys that node owned, about 1/N of them, to its neighbours. Routing uses the local view at once, but heavy rebalancing, such as streaming data to rebuild replicas, waits until a node has been dead for a while or an operator confirms. During a partition, writes need a quorum (a majority) of the replicas, so only the side that holds a majority of a key's replicas accepts them, and the smaller side refuses or serves stale reads.
steps.tradeoff: A short false alarm costs only some rerouted requests, and no data moves. The delay before rebalancing means a real failure runs with fewer replicas for longer. Choosing a quorum gives consistency during a partition, but the minority side loses availability, and a membership layer on its own cannot give both.

failures.scenario: A node freezes for eight seconds in a full garbage-collection pause
failures.impact: It stops answering pings and sending anything, so the others suspect it, and a short timeout would declare it dead and start moving its data.
failures.answer: The suspicion timeout is longer than the usual pause, and the node can refute with a higher incarnation as soon as it wakes and sees the suspect message. Pauses longer than the timeout still cause a death, which is then corrected by a rejoin with a higher incarnation, so the real fix is also to tune the heap and detect pauses. The data transfer is delayed by a grace period, so a death that is refuted within it moves nothing.

failures.scenario: The network splits a 100-node cluster into 70 and 30
failures.impact: Each side marks the other as dead, each side builds its own ring, and clients on both sides may write the same keys.
failures.answer: Membership alone cannot prevent this, because each side sees a consistent but different truth. Writes that need a quorum of replicas succeed only on the side with a majority, and the smaller side stops accepting them. When the network heals, the incarnation numbers and a full sync make the lists merge, and the data is reconciled by versions or read repair (fixing a stale copy when a read finds it).

failures.scenario: One node has a flaky network card that drops 30% of its packets
failures.impact: It keeps being suspected and refuting, so its status flaps, and each flip makes the ring reroute its keys back and forth.
failures.answer: The indirect probes avoid blaming the node for a single lossy link. The flapping is damped by making a node that keeps failing probes less trusted, and by doing no rebalancing until it has been dead continuously for the grace period. Metrics on the suspicion rate per node point an operator to the broken machine.

failures.scenario: A rolling deployment restarts 200 nodes within a minute
failures.impact: Hundreds of leave, join and suspect updates arrive at once, the piggyback buffers overflow, and some nodes see an inconsistent list for a while.
failures.answer: Graceful leaves announce themselves, so no suspicion is needed, and restarts keep their identity but get a higher incarnation. The periodic full sync repairs any update that was dropped from the buffers. Operators limit the number of nodes restarted at the same time, so the cluster never loses more replicas than the quorum allows.

failures.scenario: All the seed nodes are down while a new node tries to join
failures.impact: The new node knows nobody and cannot get the member list, so it stays outside the cluster.
failures.answer: The cluster keeps running, because seeds are not part of failure detection. The joining node retries with backoff, tries the seed list from DNS as well as from its config, and an operator can add the address of any running member. Each seed lists several other seeds, and seeds are spread over different racks and zones.

alternatives.title: How nodes check each other

options.name: A central monitor
options.pro: Easy to build and to reason about, and one place to look
options.con: A single point of failure and a bottleneck, and it sees only its own viewpoint

options.name: All-to-all heartbeats
options.pro: Fast and simple, with a decision made independently by every node
options.con: N(N-1) messages per second, and every pair is a chance for a false alarm

options.name: Gossip heartbeats
options.pro: A few messages per node, and a counter spreads through the cluster
options.con: Each message holds the whole table, and the time to detect grows with log N plus a long tail of delay

options.name: SWIM probes with suspicion
options.pro: Constant load per node, indirect probes for fewer false alarms, and small messages
options.con: More moving parts, and a probe sees only one peer's viewpoint

alternatives.pick: SWIM, as used by Consul, Serf and Nomad. Past roughly 100 nodes the other options cost too much, or are too slow or too false-alarm-prone.

alternatives.title: How long to wait before declaring a node dead

options.name: Fixed timeout
options.con: Too short during a slow patch and too long when the network is fast, and it must be re-tuned per environment

options.name: Phi-accrual
options.pro: Adapts to the observed arrival times, and gives a suspicion level rather than a yes or no
options.con: Needs a history per peer and assumes a shape for the delays, and the threshold is still a choice

options.name: Suspicion with a scaled timeout and self-awareness
options.pro: The accused can refute, and a node that is itself slow becomes more patient
options.con: A longer time to confirm a real death

alternatives.pick: Suspicion with a timeout scaled by log N for SWIM, and phi-accrual where heartbeats are the signal, as Cassandra does.

alternatives.title: Who decides what the membership is

options.name: Gossip with eventual agreement
options.pro: No coordinator, scales to thousands of nodes, and available during a partition
options.con: Views can differ for a few seconds, or for the whole partition

options.name: A consensus store such as etcd or ZooKeeper
options.pro: One agreed list at every moment, and a clear answer to who is a member
options.con: A small quorum that must stay reachable, and writes limited to what one leader can do

alternatives.pick: Gossip for liveness at scale. A small consensus group for decisions that must be unique, such as configuration or leadership.

alternatives.title: When to move data after a node looks dead

options.name: At once
options.pro: Replicas are restored soon after a real failure
options.con: Every false alarm streams gigabytes out and back

options.name: After a grace period, or by an operator
options.pro: Short blips cost nothing, and the load of repair is spread out
options.con: Fewer replicas for longer, so a second failure is more dangerous

options.name: Hand off the writes and repair later
options.pro: The cluster stays writable, and the node catches up when it returns
options.con: Hints must be stored and replayed, and are lost if their holder dies

alternatives.pick: A grace period, with hinted handoff for the writes that arrive while a node is thought to be down.

quiz.question: A database cluster has every node send a heartbeat to every other node once a second. At 100 nodes that is about 10,000 messages a second in total. The cluster is growing to 2,000 nodes. What best keeps failure detection from becoming the main load?
options: Lengthen the heartbeat interval to 20 seconds, which cuts the message rate and still lets every node check every other node
Let each node ping one random peer per round and ask a few others to retry the ping if no reply comes, at constant cost
Move heartbeats to one dedicated monitor that pings all 2,000 nodes and publishes the list of live nodes to everyone
Switch the heartbeats from UDP to TCP so that each message is acknowledged and the sender can stop after the first reply
quiz.explanation: All-to-all heartbeats cost N(N-1) messages, about 4 million a second at 2,000 nodes. Probing one random peer per round costs about the same per node at any size. A longer interval is still quadratic and slower, and a single monitor becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure.

quiz.question: A node in a gossip cluster freezes for 3 seconds in a garbage-collection pause. Peers ping it with a 1 second timeout, and indirect probes through three other nodes also time out. Today it is declared dead at once and its data starts moving. Which change cuts such false deaths while a real crash is still confirmed within a few seconds?
options: Use 10 indirect probers instead of 3, since more independent network paths make a missed reply less likely to be a real failure
Raise the failure timeout to 30 seconds for every node, so that a pause of any normal length is ignored
Declare a node dead only after a majority vote of all nodes, collected in a consensus round before any list changes
Mark a node that fails probes as suspect for a few seconds, so that it can refute with a higher incarnation number
quiz.explanation: A frozen node ignores every prober, so more probers do not help, but a suspect state gives it time to wake up and say it is alive. A 30 second timeout cures the false alarm and also delays every real crash by 30 seconds. A cluster-wide vote is heavy and not needed when the accused can refute.

quiz.question: A 100-node cluster with 3 replicas per key splits into groups of 70 and 30 nodes. Each side marks the other dead and builds its own hash ring. Clients on both sides keep writing the same keys, and each write is acknowledged by a single replica. What actually prevents both sides from accepting writes for the same key?
options: Requiring 2 of the key's 3 original replicas to acknowledge each write, so only the side holding most of them can accept it
The incarnation numbers carried in gossip, which make the 30-node side accept that the 70-node side has the newer view of the cluster
A suspicion timeout set above the longest expected partition, so that neither side ever declares the other dead before it heals
Choosing the seed node with the lowest id as owner of the whole ring, so that exactly one side keeps a valid ring
quiz.explanation: Each side holds a consistent but different view, and gossip cannot cross the partition, so membership alone cannot decide. A quorum counted over the key's original replica set, not over each side's rebuilt ring, lets only the side holding most of those replicas write and makes the other refuse. A longer suspicion timeout only delays the split, and the lowest-id seed may be on either side.
